title: 1 Chronicles 7:1–13
context: Chapter 7 continues the tribal genealogies that began in chapter 2, here covering Issachar (7:1–5), Benjamin (7:6–12), and Naphtali (7:13). Several entries record the number of fighting men, some explicitly “in the days of David” (7:2), which suggests the Chronicler drew on military registers. The names partly match the lists of Jacob’s descendants in Genesis 46 and Numbers 26, with differences in spelling and in which sons are named; Benjamin’s sons, for example, are listed differently here, in 8:1–2, and in Genesis 46:21. The text does not explain these differences, and this page does not harmonize them. Naphtali receives a single verse. Zebulun and Dan, though named among Israel’s sons in 2:1–2, receive no separate genealogy in chapters 4–8, and the text does not say why. Both traditions read these lists as shared ground: God remembers his people by name, tribe by tribe, and the Chronicler preserves that memory for a community rebuilding after exile.

verses.text: Of the sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four.
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s four sons head the list: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler begins each tribe with its founding fathers, honoring each family as part of the covenant people, with its own history before God and its own responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these names largely match Genesis 46:13 and Numbers 26:23–24, linking the post-exilic community to God’s promises to the patriarchs. Shared ground: both traditions see the genealogy as a testimony that God keeps covenant with his people across generations.

verses.text: The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers’ houses, of Tola; mighty men of valor in their generations. Their number in the days of David was twenty-two thousand six hundred.
verses.arminianNotes: Tola’s sons are heads of fathers’ houses and mighty men of valor, numbering 22,600 in David’s day. Arminian readers note that the record honors faithful service in Israel’s defense and that each generation took up its own responsibility within the people of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the link to David’s reign, a high point in Israel’s history under God’s covenant king. The numbers show God’s blessing in multiplying his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a record of God’s provision and of the tribe’s place in the kingdom.

verses.text: The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. The sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, five; all of them chief men.
verses.arminianNotes: Uzzi’s son Izrahiah and his four sons are called chief men. Arminian readers see the genealogy tracing leadership within the tribe from one generation to the next. Each man named had a real role among his people, and the record preserves his memory before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Scripture preserves even obscure names, showing that God knows his people individually. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a careful family record, and both affirm that no member of God’s people is forgotten by him, even when little more than a name survives.

verses.text: With them, by their generations, after their fathers’ houses, were bands of the army for war, thirty-six thousand; for they had many wives and sons.
verses.arminianNotes: The tribe could field 36,000 men, “for they had many wives and sons.” Arminian readers note that the Chronicler records the cause of the tribe’s growth without praising or condemning it. Large families meant military strength, which the record treats as a historical fact.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the Chronicler’s plain statement of the reason for the tribe’s size. They do not take the verse as an endorsement of polygamy, which Scripture elsewhere shows to bring trouble. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical description, not moral instruction.

verses.text: Their brothers among all the families of Issachar, mighty men of valor, listed in all by genealogy, were eighty-seven thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s families, listed by genealogy, total 87,000 mighty men. Arminian readers note the summary figure that closes the tribe’s entry. The record shows a substantial tribe ready to serve, and they do not press the numbers for theological conclusions the text does not draw.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the figure as a historical summary from the genealogical records. The text gives no comment on how the totals relate to the earlier figures. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a record of the tribe’s strength and decline to build doctrine on the counts.

verses.text: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three.
verses.arminianNotes: Benjamin’s three sons are named: Bela, Becher, and Jediael. Arminian readers note that this short list differs from 8:1–2 and Genesis 46:21, and they accept that ancient genealogies could serve different purposes and select different names without explaining why.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the different lists and do not force a harmony the text does not supply. Shared ground: both traditions affirm the trustworthiness of the record while recognizing that genealogies in Scripture are selective and that this list does not explain its relationship to others.

verses.text: The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five; heads of fathers’ houses, mighty men of valor; and they were listed by genealogy twenty-two thousand thirty-four.
verses.arminianNotes: Bela’s five sons are heads of fathers’ houses, with 22,034 registered. Arminian readers note the precise figure, which reflects the careful record-keeping of Israel’s tribes. Each household had its own leaders and its own part to play in the life of the nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler’s precision honors the reality of these families and their place in Israel’s history. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a historical register and see in it a testimony to God’s preservation of Benjamin as a tribe.

verses.text: The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher.
verses.arminianNotes: Becher’s nine sons are named, including Anathoth, which is also the name of a Benjamite town given to the priests (6:60). Arminian readers note the possible connection between family and place, though the text does not explain whether the town took its name from this man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the overlap of a personal name and a place name, without pressing a conclusion the text does not draw. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Benjamin’s family record and see God’s people rooted in real places and real households.

verses.text: They were listed by genealogy, after their generations, heads of their fathers’ houses, mighty men of valor, twenty thousand two hundred.
verses.arminianNotes: Becher’s descendants number 20,200 mighty men. Arminian readers note the repeated pattern of heads of houses and fighting strength, which shows the Chronicler drawing on registers of service. The tribe’s readiness is recorded as part of its contribution to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same pattern and note that God multiplied Benjamin despite its near destruction in Judges 20–21. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a register of strength and see in Benjamin’s survival a sign of God’s mercy to his people.

verses.text: The son of Jediael: Bilhan. The sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.
verses.arminianNotes: Jediael’s son Bilhan and his seven sons are named, one of them called Benjamin and another Ehud. Arminian readers note that names recur across generations, and they do not assume that this Ehud is the judge of Judges 3 without clearer evidence from the text.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the recurrence of familiar names within the tribe and avoid hasty identifications. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the family record and agree that it raises no theological question beyond God’s care for each household.

verses.text: All these were sons of Jediael, according to the heads of their fathers’ households, mighty men of valor, seventeen thousand two hundred, who were able to go out in the army for war.
verses.arminianNotes: Jediael’s descendants number 17,200 men able to go out to war. Arminian readers note the emphasis on readiness for service. The genealogies show tribes prepared to defend the people of God, and each man counted bore a real share of that responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same emphasis and see the tribe’s strength as God’s provision for his people’s security. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a military register and see the community’s strength as a gift to be used in service, not a ground for pride.

verses.text: So were Shuppim, Huppim, the sons of Ir, Hushim, and the sons of Aher.
verses.arminianNotes: Shuppim, Huppim, Hushim, and the sons of Ir and Aher close Benjamin’s short list. Arminian readers note that the verse is brief and that its connections are not fully explained. Some of these names also appear in other Benjamite lists, and they hold any identifications loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the brevity and uncertainty of the verse. Some readers connect Hushim with the son of Dan named in Genesis 46:23, but the text does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse cautiously and decline to build conclusions on uncertain links.

verses.text: The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, Shallum, and the sons of Bilhah.
verses.arminianNotes: Naphtali receives a single verse: four sons and “the sons of Bilhah,” Jacob’s concubine through whom Naphtali was born. Arminian readers note that even a brief entry keeps the tribe within the record of God’s people, with its own place in Israel’s story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the names largely match Genesis 46:24, again linking the community to God’s covenant with the patriarchs. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence that no tribe is forgotten, even when its record is short, and that God’s promises embrace all of Israel.
